rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account frames Pharaoh’s destruction as arising from rejection of Moses and Aaron through denial of the believer, so rejecting a messenger’s companion amounts to rejecting the messenger.
rows.anchor: denying them becomes tantamount to denying the messenger and the fate of this denial is the same as that of the denial of the messenger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s drowning was accompanied by thunder, lightning and earthquakes that destroyed Egypt’s buildings and orchards; 7:137 records this fuller punishment, since total rejection entails complete rout.
rows.anchor: The answer to this question is that two types of punishments struck the Pharaoh and his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse laments that people repeatedly mocked messengers and suffered the consequences; Quraysh repeat this pattern, and a mocked messenger becomes a scourge after first coming as great mercy.
rows.anchor: every time God sent a messenger for the guidance of people they made fun of him and then faced the evil consequences of this attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses warn Quraysh that nations who mocked messengers were destroyed beyond return in this world, and that all people will appear before God for judgment.
rows.anchor: Nations who indulge in this are routed to such an extent in this world that they can never return.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In إِنْ كُلٌّ لَمَّا, إنْ is the lightened form, marked by ل; لَمَّا fills a rhythmic gap without changing the meaning, as in 86:4.
rows.anchor: The ْنِإِ is reduced (mukhaffafah) as is evidenced by the letter ل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section III returns from the historical example to signs in the world: arrogance keeps Quraysh from seeing the abundant signs above and below them, though they demand new ones.
rows.anchor: from here on the discourse connects to the introduction of the sūrah in which it was said that their real malady

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After explaining who will benefit from the Book, the closing passage points to providential signs that call for gratitude, then reassures the Prophet to entrust opponents’ mockery to God.
rows.anchor: some very prominent signs of God’s providence are alluded to in order to once again invite people to show gratitude to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative pronoun in “We have not taught him” refers to the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the accusative pronoun in ُہاَنْمَّلَع is the Prophet (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement refutes those who called the Qur’an poetry and Muhammad a poet, using that claim to explain away its eloquence and divert people from its divine authority.
rows.anchor: This is actually a refutation of people who regard the Qur’ān to be poetry and the Prophet (sws) to be a poet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It is not befitting for him” means poetry is lower in status than prophethood; Islahi develops this through the different character and scope of poets’ and prophets’ work.
rows.anchor: The expression اَمَو يِغَنبَی ُهَل means that poetry is something of lesser in status to a prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets make grand claims without practicing them, whereas prophets most fully practice what they preach.
rows.anchor: not practice what they preach. On the contrary, a prophet practices the most

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets wander among contradictory ideas, unlike prophets, whose principles and corollaries cohere and whose speech has sequence and correspondence.
rows.anchor: Their second characteristic is that their compositions are a collection of contradictory thoughts; he wanders in every field

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Strayed people follow poets, whereas God’s prophets are followed by noble and pious people.
rows.anchor: Their third characteristic is that only people who have strayed away from the truth follow poets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic rule about poets has rare exceptions; God has protected His prophets from poetry’s harmful influence.
rows.anchor: For this reason, the Almighty has protected his prophets from the evil touch of poetry.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry arises from and affects emotions, while prophethood addresses every sphere through intellect, moral correction, life principles and statecraft; such guidance requires a clear divine book.
rows.anchor: all poetry relates to emotions: it arises from emotions and also effects emotions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David’s Psalms supplement the Torah with prayers, sermons and wise counsel; they are a blessed treasury with the Torah but cannot alone fulfill a messenger’s guidance mission.
rows.anchor: The status of the Psalms is that of an addendum to the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a reminder, the Qur’an recalls innate truths, the history of divine guidance from Adam to Muhammad, and the worldly and otherworldly consequences of rejecting messengers.
rows.anchor: It reminds people of the facts innately found in human nature; it also reminds people of the history of divine guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Clear Qur’an” describes a comprehensive guide with unambiguous, reasoned counsel for every part of life, whose clarity leaves a fair-minded person with no doubt.
rows.anchor: It explains every fact so clearly that no doubt remains in the mind of a fair person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of “that it may warn” is the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: The subject of the verb َرِنذُی is the Prophet Muh@ammad (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an was revealed to warn the intellectually and spiritually alive; those with dead hearts will not benefit, but the truth is conveyed conclusively so disbelievers have no excuse.
rows.anchor: the truth shall stand conclusively conveyed to them and they will not be able to present this excuse before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warning has its full force for people whose hearts are alive and responsive; Islahi cites 36:11 and 35:22 to contrast those who heed with the spiritually dead.
rows.anchor: The verb انذار warning) here is in its complete meaning and the word ّيَحٌ refers to those whose hearts are alive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s phrasing reassures the Prophet that his task is to awaken the living, not the spiritually dead, a recurring Qur’anic theme.
rows.anchor: The style adopted in the verse under discussion sounds an assurance to the Prophet (sws) as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusive “word” against disbelievers refers to God’s earlier promise to reveal guidance to Adam’s progeny and punish those who follow Satan despite it.
rows.anchor: the truth shall stand conclusively conveyed to them and they will not be able to present this excuse before God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage repeats the sequence of 33–35: after the Qur’an’s warning and monotheism, signs of providence are shown and people are called to gratitude.
rows.anchor: here too after directing their attention to certain signs of God’s providence that substantiate the preaching of the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what God’s hands made echoes the wording in 36:35 and points to divine power and wisdom as the source of these creatures.
rows.anchor: The expression اَّمِم ْتَلِمَع اَنیِدْیَأُ implies the same thing as what expression َو مَا ْتَلِمَعُه یِدْیَأُْمِه that occurred earlier in verse 35 implied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The beasts’ existence and human mastery show that only God’s power and wisdom could create and subjugate them; this blessing calls people to consider their responsibility and gratitude.
rows.anchor: The implication is that this situation invites man to reflect whether this great blessing of God imposes any responsibility on him or not?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making the animals subject to human use is God’s gracious provision, enabled by His power and wisdom.
rows.anchor: no other being could dare do so or bring them into man’s subservience.
